summary:
North Jeolla Province has no separate local ordinance on gender identity or gender expression, so a visitor stands under the national framework of South Korea. Being transgender is not criminalised and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The only criminalisation in this field sits in the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 punishes consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, a provision the Constitutional Court upheld in 2023, and transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Legal gender recognition operates province-wide and no longer depends on surgery. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants who had not undergone sex-reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine a gender change based on surgery and that judicial guidelines requiring surgery are now reference material rather than criteria. The court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity.

Restroom access is protected by rulings that bind North Jeolla as national law. On 22 July 2024 an Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a claim of 3 million won, ruling that police advice telling a person who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020 to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights; the court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. In 2021 the Daegu District Court, Pohang branch, awarded 7 million won against a beauty academy that had prohibited a transgender student from using its restroom. No incident of this kind is documented within North Jeolla.
tangentialFactors:
The national backdrop is one of documented hostility alongside incremental judicial protection. Enforcement against military personnel has been punitive: in 2017 the military charged 32 personnel in what Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, and Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after her gender-affirming surgery was classified as a handicap; the Daejeon District Court reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021 and the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty in March 2024. She died by suicide in March 2021.

South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, and a landmark 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the main advance in that area.

Violence and hostility concentrate at public events. At an Incheon Pride event about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, after which organisers filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction; Busan's 2018 Pride deployed some 2,000 police to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people and doxing and online harassment rose.

Survey data indicate the scale of everyday discrimination: 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates in a 2014 finding, 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, and a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the past year. A peer-reviewed nationwide survey of 585 transgender and non-binary young adults published in Epidemiology and Health on 27 June 2025 documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care.
localsOnly:
Residents of North Jeolla can obtain a change of registered sex without having undergone sex-reassignment surgery, the Yeongdong ruling having removed the surgical prerequisite as national law province-wide, and court guidelines that once demanded surgery now serve only as reference.

Police conduct toward residents in the province is constrained by the appellate judgment of 22 July 2024, which treated advice to avoid public restrooms of one's gender as an infringement of personal rights and awarded compensation against the state. Provincial schools, academies and similar premises face monetary liability for barring a transgender person from a restroom, as the beauty academy did in the 2021 Daegu District Court, Pohang branch, judgment.

The National Human Rights Commission of Korea's 2021 survey of 591 transgender respondents gives the practical context residents live with: 41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink to do so, and 36% simply forwent restroom use.
outOfScopeNotes:
No incident of restroom-related discrimination or police interference is documented within North Jeolla itself; the restroom findings above come from courts in Seoul and in another province and are reported as national law applying to the province rather than as events that occurred here.

The province-level record carries no sourcing on trans-specific healthcare availability, hospital admission practice or the outcome of the Ministry of Health and Welfare's refusal in November 2023 to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, beyond the National Human Rights Commission of Korea's identification of that blind spot at national level.

Whether North Jeolla's schools or provincial education authorities have issued guidance on restroom and facilities access for transgender students is not sourced. The youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong's findings of 20 March 2024 on students avoiding school restrooms are national research, with no provincial breakdown supplied.

Hate-crime sentencing enhancement and any province-specific anti-discrimination measures are not addressed in the available material, and the relationship between the absence of a comprehensive national anti-discrimination law and enforcement practice within North Jeolla remains unverified.
